Surah al-Humaza

Makki, and its verses are nine, without disagreement on either point. When Allah, glory be to Him, had mentioned in what preceded it that mankind, except those who are exempted, are in loss, He, mighty and majestic, explained in this surah the states of some of the losers, so the Mighty One said:

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer.﴾ The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this kind of sentence has already passed. Al-hamz means breaking, like crushing (al-hazm), and al-lamz means fault-finding, like al-lahz. Both became common in the sense of breaking/attacking people's honour, belittling them, backbiting them, and defaming them. Originally this was a metaphor, since breaking and literal striking cannot be conceived of in bodies, and it became a conventional literal meaning. The pattern fu'ala indicates habituation, so one does not say dahakah (one who laughs a lot) or la'anah (one who curses a lot) except for one who does it much and is accustomed to it. Ziyad al-A'jam said:

"When I meet you from a distance, you grin at me, but when I am absent, you are the one who slanders and backbites."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group [of narrators] related from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about this and said: It is the one who walks about with tale-bearing, who separates the united, and who incites between brothers.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abd ibn Humayd and others related from Mujahid: the humaza is the one who defames people, and the lumaza is the one who defames lineages.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Abu al-Aliya: al-hamz is to someone's face and al-lamz is behind their back. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ibn Jurayj: al-hamz is with the eye, the cheek and the hand, and al-lamz is with the tongue. It has been said otherwise, but what has preceded is comprehensive.

Al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "Woe to every humzah lumzah" with a sukun on the mim in both, in the common pattern meaning the object, namely the mocked one who brings jokes so that people laugh at him, and who is insulted, belittled and mocked. This was revealed concerning what Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of Ibn Ishaq from Uthman ibn Umar concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf; and concerning what he related from al-Suddi concerning Ubayy ibn Amr al-Thaqafi, famous as al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, for he was a frequent backbiter and much given to disparagement; and concerning what Ibn Ishaq said about Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, who used to belittle the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and disparage him; and concerning what Ibn Jarir and others related from Mujahid about Jamil ibn Amir; and concerning what has been said about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his backbiting of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his disparaging of him; and according to one opinion, concerning al-As ibn Wa'il. It is possible that it was revealed concerning all of those mentioned. However, the revelation concerning al-Akhnas has been questioned: according to what Ibn Hajar authenticated in al-Isaba, he embraced Islam and was among those whose hearts were to be reconciled, so the threat that follows cannot apply to him. Either that report is not sound, or his Islam is not sound. Also, al-Baqir's reading has been questioned on the basis of what you have heard about its meaning, and the revelation concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and the like of the great men of Quraysh. With this, what is raised in the interpretations is answered, namely how the disbeliever is censured with these two acts when in him there is a state more ugly than them, which is disbelief. As for what was answered, that disbelief is not ugly in itself unlike them, its weakness is not hidden, because losing correct belief is uglier than every ugly thing.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 104, verse 2:

Allah's words, ﴿Who has gathered wealth﴾, are a substitution (badal) from "kull" (every), a substitution of the whole (badal kull), and it has been said that it is a substitution of part from whole (badal ba'd min kull). Al-Jarbardi said: it may be an adjective (sifah) for it, because it is definite (ma'rifah), according to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned concerning Allah's words, ﴿And every soul will come with it a driver and a witness﴾, since he made the clause "ma'aha sa'iq" (with it a driver) a circumstantial clause (hal) from "kull nafs" (every soul) for that reason. And what is in it is not hidden.

It may also be in the accusative or nominative case, as a censure (dhamm). The indefiniteness of "mal" (wealth) is for magnification (tafkhim) and abundance (takthir). According to those who said it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas, he had four thousand dinars, and it was said ten thousand. It is also permitted that it is for belittlement (tahqir) and minimization (taqlil), considering that before Allah it is the least and most worthless of things.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read "jammaa" with a doubled mim, for intensification (takthir), and this is more suitable to Allah's words ﴿and counted it﴾, i.e., he counted it again and again, out of love for it and passion for it. It was said: he made it into kinds and types, such as property and cash, related by al-Ta'wilat. And many others said: i.e., he made it a reserve and a store for the calamities and misfortunes of time.

Al-Hasan and al-Kalbi read "wa-'addadah" with a light pronunciation (takhfif). It was said its meaning is "wa-'addahu," so it is a past-tense verb whose doubling was unbound (fukka idghamuhu) contrary to analogy, as in the verse:

Gently, O my blamer, have you tested in my character
That I am generous to people even when they are stingy.

It was also said that it is a noun meaning the known number ('adad), conjoined with "malahu" (his wealth), i.e., he gathered his wealth and fixed its number and counted it. This is not, according to al-Kashf, of the type of "'alaftuha tibnan wa-ma'an barida" (I fed her straw and cold water), because gathering a number is an expression for controlling and counting it, so it needs no strained interpretation. On both readings, the first meaning is supported by the mentioned reading of the majority (jumhur). It was also said that it is a noun meaning followers and helpers, as one says: "So-and-so has a large 'adad or 'udad" if he has a substantial number of helpers and those who support him; it is conjoined with "malahu" as well, i.e., he gathered his wealth and his people who support him.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 104, verse 3:**

﴿He thinks that his wealth has made him immortal.﴾ It is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*) or a resumptive clause (*jumla isti'nafiyya*). *Akhladahu* and *khalladahu* have the same meaning: he made him remain (*tarakahu khaliden*), that is, lasting (*makithan*) in a stay that has no end, or a very long stay. The statement is of the type of the allegorical metaphor (*al-isti'ara al-tamthiliyya*). The meaning is that wealth lengthened his hope and gave him distant wishes, so he acts, in building structures, planting trees, digging rivers and the like, as one who thinks that his wealth has kept him alive.

The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun (*al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar*) is for emphasis, and the use of the past tense is for intensifying the intended meaning.

It is also permitted that the intended meaning is that he truly reckons this, because of his extreme delusion and his preoccupation with accumulating and multiplying [wealth], so that he is distracted from the calamities of the Hereafter that lie ahead of him. Or it is because he assumes that life and safety from illnesses and afflictions depend on observing apparent causes, and that wealth is the axis of its revolution and the ruler obeyed in its city.

It has been said: the meaning is that he considers wealth among the things that confer immortality, and there is no regard to whether immortality is worldly or otherworldly, in mention or in fact. The concern is only with establishing this property for wealth. The purpose of this is an allusion (*ta'rid*) that there is an immortal thing which the intelligent person should devote himself to, namely striving for the Hereafter. But this is very remote, and for this reason some of the eminent scholars did not make the allusion a separate interpretation.

Isam al-Din claimed that it is possible that the subject of *akhlada* is the reckoner (*al-hasib*) and its object is wealth, meaning: he thinks that he will preserve his wealth forever, and does not realize that it is exposed to misfortunes or to separation through death, as it has been said: "Give good news to the miser's wealth of a misfortune or an heir." By my life, this is something for which Isam has no excuse.

﴿Nay!﴾ is a rebuke to him for that baseless reckoning, or for that and for his gathering of wealth and his excessive love of it, as has been said. It has also been favoured that it is a rebuke for mocking and slandering (al-hamz wa'l-lamz), though this has been criticised as far-fetched both in wording and in meaning. I see no harm in it being a rebuke for everything the preceding clauses contained of ugly qualities.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He will surely be thrown﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, and the clause is a resumptive clause (istinaf) explaining the reason for the rebuke. That is: by God, he will surely be cast, because of his deeds mentioned above, ﴿into the Crusher﴾, that is, into the Fire, which by its nature crushes everyone thrown into it. The pattern fu'alah is used to present the act, as it is natural, as if it were habitual. Al-hatm is the breaking of a thing, like al-hashm, and then it was used for any thorough breaking. They recited:

"We struck Mus'ab with the rod on the day we broke his nose, so that he would be angry."

It is said: a man is a huthamah, that is, a great eater, likening him to the Fire; and for this reason it was said of a great eater that it is as if there were an oven in his belly. Al-Dahhak interpreted al-Hutamah here as the fourth level of the Fire. Al-Kalbi said: it is the sixth tier of Hell. Al-Qushayri related from him that it is the second level. Al-Wahidi said: it is one of the gates of Hell. Abu Salih claimed that it is the fire that is in their graves, but this is nothing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 104, verse 5:

The saying of He, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what is the Huṭamah?﴾ is for magnifying its matter, by explaining that it is not among the things which the minds of creation can attain.

ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Ḥasan, in a variant reading from him, and Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ḥumayd, and Hārūn from Abū ʿAmr, read: «liyunbadhāni» (﴿they two shall surely be thrown﴾), with the dual pronoun referring to the Humazah and her wealth. And from al-Ḥasan also: «liyunbadhunna» with a ḍammah on the dhāl and deletion of the plural pronoun. It was said: it refers to every Humazah, considering that the term is plural in meaning; and it was said: it refers to him and to his number, that is, his followers and helpers, on the basis of what you have heard in his reading there.

From Abū ʿAmr: «lananbidhannahu» with the nūn of majesty, a pronoun of the accusative (hāʾ), and the emphatic nūn. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, read: «fī al-ḥāṭimah, wa-mā adrāka mā al-ḥāṭimah» (﴿in the Ḥāṭimah. And what will make you know what is the Ḥāṭimah?﴾).

"Fire of Allah" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence serves to clarify the status of what is being asked about. That is, it is the fire of Allah, ﴿kindled﴾ by the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In attributing it to Him, glorified is He, and in describing it as kindled, there is a magnification of its matter beyond which nothing more can be said.

﴿Which mounts over the hearts﴾: that is, it rises to the midst of the hearts and envelops them. The heart (fu'ad) is singled out for mention because it is the most refined part of the body and the most sensitive to pain from the slightest harm that touches it. Or it is because it is the seat of deviant beliefs, corrupt intentions, and ugly dispositions, and the source of evil deeds. Thus it is the most fitting of all the parts of the body mentioned earlier.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that he said concerning the verse: "It consumes everything of him until it reaches his heart. When it reaches his heart, his creation begins (anew)." It is also permissible that what is meant is cognitive surveying (al-ittila' al-'ilmi), and that the speech is figurative. That is because, since each of the tormented has a punishment from the fire according to the measure of his sin, which arises from the qualities of his heart, it was said that the fire surveys the hearts, which are the mines of sins, so it knows what is in them and recompenses each according to the attribute within him that calls for punishment.

The people of allusion (ishara, esoteric hints) say: what has been mentioned is an allusion to the spiritual punishment, which is the most severe punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 104, verses 8–9:

﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾, i.e., sealed shut. The complete discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-Balad.

﴿In extended columns﴾: ʿamad is the plural of ʿamud (pillar), as al-Raghib and al-Farra' said. Abu ʿUbayda said it is the plural of ʿimad. In al-Bahr, it is said that it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ), whose singular is ʿamud. Al-Akhawan and Abu Bakr read ﴿ʿumud﴾ with two dammas, and Harun, from Abu ʿAmr, read it with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the mim. In both readings it is the plural of ʿamud, without any disagreement. The words ﴿mumaddada﴾ (extended) describe ʿamad in all three readings, meaning tall. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿ʿalayhim﴾ (upon them), meaning: they will be confined in extended columns, i.e., bound within them, like stocks (al-maqatir). These are large beams or trunks of wood with holes in which the feet of imprisoned thieves and the like are placed. Alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they will be in columns in which they are bound. And these, may God protect us, are, as narrated from Ibn Zayd, columns of iron. Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are of fire. Some have inferred that the columns are stretched across the doors after they have been sealed over them, as a confirmation of their despair and a double securing of their confinement.

In a lengthy hadith, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related in Nawadir al-Usul from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "God, exalted is He, after bringing out of the Fire the sinful believers, and those who remain in it longest, those who will remain for seven thousand years, will send, mighty and majestic is He, angels to the people of the Fire with lids of fire, nails of fire, and columns of fire. They will be closed over them with those lids, fastened with those nails, and those columns will be extended, and no gap will remain through which a spirit may enter or any distress may leave. The Almighty, mighty and majestic, will forget them upon His Throne, and the people of Paradise will be occupied with their bliss. They will never call for help after that, speech will cease, and their speech will be only groaning and sobbing."

Within it: that is the meaning of His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾ ﴿in extended columns﴾. O God, protect us from the Fire, O best of those sought for protection.

On this reading, the prepositional phrase is attached to ﴿mu'sada﴾ (closed) as a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun within it, as the author of al-Kashf said and al-Tibi related. In al-Irshad, from Abu al-Baqa', it is said that it is a qualifier of ﴿mu'sada﴾. Some said: there is no objection to its being a complement (silah) of ﴿mu'sada﴾, in the sense that the doors are closed with the columns and sealed by them. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said regarding the verse: He will place them in columns, and chains will be stretched around their necks, and the doors will be secured with them.

Moreover, what has been mentioned, by its indication of eternal abiding and the severity of punishment, suits the view that those spoken of are disbelievers who insulted and defamed the best of mankind, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. As for the earlier interpretation of the columns as stocks, it was said that it suits the general sense, since the backbiter is like a thief stealing people's honour, so it is fitting that he be punished with stocks like thieves, and thus eternal abiding is not necessarily implied. It may also be said: whoever reflects on this surah will see a wondrous and marvellous harmony. When intensification was expressed in the description ﴿scorner, slanderer﴾, it was followed by ﴿al-Hutama﴾ (the crusher) for balance. Since this implied the breaking of honour, it was countered by the breaking of bones indicated by al-Hutama. The word "nabdh" (being cast off), which signals contempt, was used to oppose the dignity the scorner and slanderer imagined for himself. Since the source of gathering wealth is the domination of love for it over the heart, the counterpart was ﴿It rises over the hearts﴾. Since it is the nature of a wealth-gatherer who loves it to lock it up, the counterpart was ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾. And since this implies prolonged hope, the counterpart was ﴿in extended columns﴾. Some of the eminent scholars have stated this explicitly, so let it be pondered. And God knows best.
